questions.prompt: Is a signed JWT encrypted?

options.text: No — it is only Base64url-encoded and readable by anyone; the signature only proves integrity
Yes — the payload is fully encrypted and secret
Yes — only the server can read any part of it
No — but the payload cannot be read without the private key

questions.explanation: A signed JWT's payload is just Base64url-encoded and readable by anyone; the signature makes it tamper-evident (if verified), not confidential — so never put secrets in it.

questions.prompt: Match each session-cookie attribute to what it protects against.

pairs.right: The cookie traveling over plaintext HTTP
The cookie being sent on cross-site requests (CSRF)

questions.explanation: HttpOnly hides the cookie from scripts, Secure keeps it off HTTP, and SameSite blocks cross-site sending — together hardening the session ID.

questions.prompt: What must a server always do with a JWT it receives? Select all that apply.

options.text: Verify the signature
Check the expiry (exp) claim
Pin the expected algorithm (reject 'none')
Trust the claims without checking, since it looks valid

questions.explanation: The server must verify the signature, check expiry (and issuer/audience), and pin the algorithm; trusting an unverified token lets an attacker forge claims.

questions.prompt: To defeat session fixation, the server should ____ the session ID at login.
questions.explanation: Regenerating the session ID at login ensures an attacker-set ID from before login can't be reused to ride the authenticated session.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to set up a secure server-side session.

items.text: Create a session with a long random ID
Issue the ID in an HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite cookie

questions.explanation: A secure session uses a random ID, a hardened cookie, ID regeneration on login, and destruction on logout — giving real revocation.

questions.prompt: Which standard should you use to authenticate a user ('sign in with...')?

options.text: OpenID Connect (an identity layer over OAuth 2.0)
Raw OAuth 2.0 access tokens as proof of identity
A plain session cookie with no server record
Base64 encoding of the username

questions.explanation: OAuth 2.0 delegates authorization, not identity; OpenID Connect adds an ID token to actually authenticate the user, so use OIDC for login.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between an IDS and an IPS?

options.text: An IDS detects and alerts; an IPS sits inline and can block traffic
An IDS blocks traffic; an IPS only logs it
They are identical
An IDS encrypts traffic; an IPS decrypts it

questions.explanation: An IDS monitors and raises alerts; an IPS sits inline and can actively block malicious traffic in real time.

questions.prompt: A good firewall policy denies traffic by ____ and allows only what is needed.
questions.explanation: Following fail-safe defaults, a firewall should deny by default and explicitly allow only required ports and sources.

questions.prompt: Match each network control to its role.

pairs.right: Controls which traffic may pass between networks
Limits how far an intruder can spread
Encrypted tunnel for secure remote access

questions.explanation: Firewalls gate traffic, segmentation contains intrusions, VPNs secure remote connections, and WAFs filter web attacks as defense in depth.

questions.prompt: Which help contain an intruder who gets a foothold? Select all that apply.

options.text: Network segmentation (VLANs, DMZ)
Least-privilege access between systems
Micro-segmentation / zero-trust networking
A single flat network with no internal boundaries

questions.explanation: Segmentation, least privilege, and micro-segmentation limit an intruder's blast radius; a flat network lets one foothold reach everything.

questions.prompt: Order the path of a request through a segmented network to the internal database.
questions.explanation: Traffic passes the perimeter firewall into the DMZ, then a second firewall before reaching the internal network — so a breached web server isn't next to the database.

questions.prompt: Why is a WAF not a substitute for fixing vulnerable code?

options.text: It filters known patterns but can be bypassed; the underlying flaw remains
A WAF automatically rewrites insecure code
WAFs only work on encrypted traffic
WAFs replace the need for HTTPS

questions.explanation: A WAF is a perimeter filter that novel encodings can bypass; it's defense in depth, not a cure for the vulnerable code (e.g. use parameterized queries).

questions.prompt: Why is timely patching one of the highest-value security controls?

options.text: Attackers quickly weaponize known vulnerabilities and scan for unpatched systems
Patches make software run faster
It removes the need for backups
Only patched systems can use encryption

questions.explanation: Most attacks reuse publicly known vulnerabilities and scan the internet for unpatched systems, so prompt patching removes the exact doors they use.

questions.prompt: Encrypting a laptop's storage so a lost or stolen device stays confidential is called full-disk ____.
questions.explanation: Full-disk encryption (BitLocker, FileVault, LUKS) protects data at rest, so device theft doesn't become a data breach.

questions.prompt: Match each hardening action to what it reduces.

pairs.right: Risk of data loss on device theft

questions.explanation: Each hardening step targets a specific weakness: fewer services, less privilege, secure baselines, and protected data at rest.

questions.prompt: Which are good endpoint-hardening practices? Select all that apply.

options.text: Automate security updates and prioritize internet-facing systems
Use standard accounts for daily work and elevate per action
Remove default credentials and unused services
Make every user a local administrator for convenience

questions.explanation: Automated updates, least-privilege accounts, and removing defaults/unused services harden endpoints; making everyone admin maximizes blast radius.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to harden a new internet-facing server.

items.text: Disable unused services and close unneeded ports
Set up least-privilege accounts (no shared admin)
Apply a hardening baseline and enable the host firewall

questions.explanation: Patch first, reduce attack surface, tighten accounts, then apply a secure baseline and firewall — each step removes exposure or caps damage.

questions.prompt: Why should daily work use a standard (non-admin) account?

options.text: If malware runs, it inherits only limited rights, capping the damage
Standard accounts cannot be phished
Admin accounts are slower
It disables the need for patching

questions.explanation: Running as a standard user means malware executing in that context inherits limited privileges, greatly reducing what it can do compared with admin.

questions.prompt: Which OWASP Top 10 (2021) category covers missing logging and monitoring?

options.text: A09 — Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
A01 — Broken Access Control
A03 — Injection
It is not in the OWASP Top 10

questions.explanation: Security Logging and Monitoring Failures is A09:2021; without them, attacks go undetected and become long, silent breaches.

questions.prompt: Which events should a security-conscious application log? Select all that apply.

options.text: Login successes and failures
Access denials and privilege changes
Creation/deletion of important data and admin changes
Users' plaintext passwords

questions.explanation: Log authentication, authorization (including denials), and important actions — but never log secrets like passwords or tokens.

questions.prompt: Logs must never contain ____ such as passwords, tokens, or full card numbers.
questions.explanation: Logs are sensitive; recording secrets or excessive personal data turns a helpful log into a new breach.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its purpose.

pairs.right: Preserves evidence off a host an attacker can wipe
Lets events from many systems line up

questions.explanation: Centralization preserves evidence, clock sync enables correlation, a SIEM correlates and alerts, and ATT&CK maps detection coverage to attacker behavior.

questions.prompt: Order these logged events into the timeline of an account-takeover attempt.

items.text: Many failed logins for one account
A successful login from a new IP
The account's role is changed to admin

questions.explanation: Correlating failures, a success, a privilege change, and exfiltration builds the story a SIEM rule can alert on — none of which any single log proves alone.

questions.prompt: What is 'alert fatigue' and how is it reduced?

options.text: Desensitization from too many low-value alerts; reduce it by tuning and prioritizing
A hardware failure in the SIEM; reduce it by rebooting
Alerts arriving too slowly; reduce it by logging less
Encryption of alerts; reduce it by disabling TLS

questions.explanation: Too many noisy alerts cause analysts to ignore them and miss the real one; tuning out false positives and prioritizing by severity restores signal.

questions.prompt: When is threat modeling most valuable, and why?

options.text: During design, because flaws are cheapest to fix before they're built
Only after a breach, to assign blame
Only in production, once real traffic arrives
Never — it is purely academic

questions.explanation: Threat modeling in design catches insecure design (OWASP A04) early, when fixes cost a fraction of the same flaw found in production.

questions.prompt: Order the four questions of threat modeling.

items.text: What are we going to do about it?
Did we do a good job?

questions.explanation: The framework models the system, enumerates threats, decides mitigations, and then reviews the work.

questions.prompt: Match each STRIDE threat to the property it violates.
questions.explanation: STRIDE maps threats to violated properties: spoofing↔auth, tampering↔integrity, information disclosure↔confidentiality, elevation↔authorization (repudiation↔non-repudiation, DoS↔availability).

questions.prompt: Which are valid responses to an identified risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: Mitigate (add a control)
Eliminate (remove the risky feature)
Transfer (shift the risk)
Accept (consciously accept and document a low risk)

questions.explanation: A threat can be mitigated, eliminated, transferred, or accepted — the choice depends on the risk and the organization's appetite.

questions.prompt: On a data-flow diagram, threats concentrate where data crosses a ____ boundary.
questions.explanation: Trust boundaries (e.g. browser to server) are where untrusted data becomes dangerous, so that's where authentication, authorization, and validation are needed.

questions.prompt: What does the STRIDE 'R' (Repudiation) threat concern?

options.text: Someone denying an action because there's no audit trail
Overwhelming a service so it's unavailable
Reading data you shouldn't
Pretending to be another user

questions.explanation: Repudiation is the ability to deny an action; it's countered by non-repudiation controls like tamper-evident audit logging.

questions.prompt: Why is a CVSS base score not the same as your risk?

options.text: CVSS measures intrinsic severity; risk also depends on exposure, asset value, and active exploitation
CVSS already includes your specific environment perfectly
Risk is always exactly the CVSS score
CVSS only applies to physical security

questions.explanation: CVSS scores intrinsic severity; a Critical on an unreachable system may pose less risk than a Medium on your internet-facing crown jewel.

questions.prompt: Match each reference to what it is.

pairs.right: Catalog of vulnerabilities exploited in the wild

questions.explanation: A CVE names a flaw, CVSS scores its severity, CWE names the weakness type, and the CISA KEV catalog lists vulnerabilities known to be exploited.

questions.prompt: Order the vulnerability-management lifecycle stages.
questions.explanation: The continuous loop runs inventory → scan → prioritize → remediate → verify — you can't secure what you don't know you have.

questions.prompt: Which signals should inform how you prioritize a vulnerability? Select all that apply.

options.text: CVSS severity
Whether it is actively exploited (CISA KEV / EPSS)
The asset's exposure and business value
The alphabetical order of the CVE ID

questions.explanation: Prioritize with severity plus real exploitation and exposure/asset value; the CVE's alphabetical order is irrelevant.

questions.prompt: The CISA ____ catalog lists vulnerabilities known to be exploited in the wild and should be fixed first.
questions.explanation: The CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog flags flaws confirmed exploited, the strongest urgency signal for patching.

questions.prompt: How does vulnerability scanning differ from penetration testing?

options.text: Scanning is automated breadth; a pen test is skilled manual depth that chains flaws to prove impact
They are identical activities
Scanning finds more exploitable chains than a pen test
A pen test never requires authorization

questions.explanation: Scanning gives automated breadth across many known issues; penetration testing adds manual depth, chaining weaknesses to demonstrate real, exploitable impact.

questions.prompt: Which document type defines the high-level security objectives and 'why'?

options.text: Policy
Standard
Procedure
Guideline

questions.explanation: A policy defines what must be done and why at a high level, setting the direction for standards and procedures.

questions.prompt: Match each risk treatment to its definition.

pairs.right: Document and live with the risk

questions.explanation: Treatment choices map to reducing, sharing, stopping, or formally accepting risk.

questions.prompt: What are the core steps of the risk management cycle? Select all that apply.

options.text: Identify
Assess
Treat
Monitor

questions.explanation: Risk management is a continuous cycle of identification, assessment, treatment, and monitoring.

questions.prompt: Order the governance document hierarchy (most to least mandatory).
questions.explanation: Governance flows from high-level mandatory policies down to specific procedures and optional best-practice guidelines.

questions.prompt: Why is compliance not the same as security?

options.text: Compliance is a baseline audit floor; security requires continuous risk management
They are the same thing
Compliance replaces security
Security is only for audits

questions.explanation: Compliance shows you met a baseline requirement at a point in time; attackers don't respect audits, and real security requires continuous risk reduction.

questions.prompt: Data ____ is the privacy principle that you should collect only the personal data you need.
questions.explanation: Data minimization means collecting the minimum personal data required for your purpose, reducing risk and compliance burden.

questions.prompt: Which of these are recognized security frameworks? Select all that apply.

options.text: NIST CSF
GDPR
SOC 2

questions.explanation: NIST CSF, ISO 27001, and SOC 2 are frameworks (maps); GDPR is a privacy law (regulation).

questions.prompt: What is 'residual risk'?

options.text: The risk remaining after controls are applied, accepted by leadership
The total initial risk
Risk that was mitigated completely
Risk you don't know about

questions.explanation: Residual risk is what is left after controls are in place; it must be consciously accepted (or further treated) by leadership.
